har2: You do not need to go to a gym to get the benefits of activity. Here are the World Health Organization's recommendations and the latest evidence on daily steps and short bursts of activity spread through the day. You can also work out your own week with the meter below.

har29: What does the World Health Organization recommend?
har30: The recommendations, updated in 2020, stress that activity brings benefits at any age and in any amount: a little activity is better than none.
har31: Adults: 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity a week, or an equivalent mix of the two.
har32: Muscle strengthening: exercises that work all the major muscle groups, on at least 2 days a week.
har33: 65 and over: in addition, activities that train balance and strength together to prevent falls, on at least 3 days a week.
har34: Sitting time: limit long spells of sitting and replace them with activity of any intensity.

har43: A study of 25,241 people who did not exercise, with an average age of 62, used wrist-worn devices to measure short, brisk bursts of activity during everyday life. Over an average follow-up of 7 years, people who did 3 short bursts of 1–2 minutes a day had a 38–40% lower risk of death from any cause and from cancer, and a 48–49% lower risk of death from cardiovascular disease, than those who did none.

har53: Do I need to take 10,000 steps a day?
har54: No. In a 2025 review that pooled 57 studies, people who took 7,000 steps a day had a 47% lower risk of death than those who took 2,000, and this benefit was very close to that seen at 10,000 steps. For some outcomes, the benefit levels off after 7,000 steps. If you take few steps, every increase is worthwhile.
har55: Do housework and climbing stairs count?
har56: Yes. The World Health Organization stresses that all activity counts. In a study that followed more than 25,000 people who did not exercise, those who did three short, brisk bursts of activity of 1–2 minutes a day (such as climbing stairs or walking very fast) had a markedly lower risk of death.
har57: Do I need a gym for muscle strengthening?
har58: No. Sit-to-stands from a chair, wall push-ups, resistance band exercises or carrying heavy shopping bags also work your muscles. What matters is working all the major muscle groups until they feel tired, on at least 2 days a week.
har59: I do no activity at all. Where should I start?
har60: A little activity is better than none. Start small and build up the time, how often and how hard you go; for example, you could start with a short daily walk and add a few minutes each week. If you have heart disease or a new symptom, talk to your doctor first.
har61: Caution: If you get chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness or palpitations during activity, stop and see a doctor. If you have heart disease, talk to your doctor before starting a new programme.
